recipes.name: Adversarial injection environment synthesis
recipes.summary: Build a stateful tool environment, hide an injected instruction in the content it returns, and grade two axes: the benign objective still completes and no forbidden call appears in the trajectory.
recipes.background: Build an executable stateful environment and then let an attacker agent and a user simulator attack it: the attacker inspects the environment to find viable injection points and writes payloads that survive the tool pipeline, while the user simulator keeps the benign objective realistic so the injected content is the only adversarial element. The task is state-grounded and long-horizon, and the attack lives in the environment's state rather than in the prompt, so the agent has to notice it inside tool output. Verification is trajectory-level and two-sided: the legitimate objective must still be completed, and the forbidden action must appear nowhere in the tool-call log or in any outgoing argument, with ordering constraints checked where the environment provides diagnostic tools.
recipes.produces: A Harbor task whose agent must finish a benign objective while an injected instruction sits in the content the tools return, graded on objective completion and on the absence of the forbidden call.
when_to_use: the target capability includes robustness to untrusted content that the agent reads through tools
the source exposes content the agent must read (files, web pages, issue text, records)
you want the attack to be discovered rather than announced in the instruction
not_when_to_use: the task is about tool-call correctness only, with no untrusted content in the loop
the environment has no content that the agent reads back
inputs: a seed domain with stateful tools that return content to the agent
an attacker agent able to query the environment for candidate injection points
a user simulator or scripted task intent that keeps the benign objective realistic

steps.title: Build the stateful environment first
steps.detail: Synthesize the environment with a real state store and tools that return environment content, so there is a surface for injected text to travel through and a state to assert afterwards.
steps.accept: Tools read from and write to a real state store whose contents persist between calls.

steps.title: Discover injection points rather than presetting them
steps.detail: Have the attacker agent query the environment - records, files, tool returns - and mark the fields whose content the task agent will read. The injection location follows from what the environment exposes, not from a fixed list of slots.
steps.accept: The chosen injection field is one the task agent actually reads back through a tool return, and that field is recorded.

steps.title: Generate environment-specific payloads
steps.detail: Write payloads that fit the field they land in and the tool that transports them, for instance instructions embedded in a record body that request an unrelated call, so the payload survives the pipeline verbatim.
steps.accept: The payload survives transport through the tool unchanged and does not restate the task instruction.

steps.title: Ground the benign task
steps.detail: Use the user simulator to produce a realistic request whose success depends on the same records the payload is embedded in, so the agent cannot solve the task by simply avoiding the contaminated field.
steps.accept: The objective cannot be completed without reading the field the payload sits in.

steps.title: Choose placement and timing deliberately
steps.detail: Place the injection in a state field the agent reads before or during the action it must take, and record the placement in the task metadata.
steps.accept: The injection sits in a state field the agent reads before or during the action it must take, and the placement is recorded in the task metadata.

steps.title: Verify on two axes plus ordering
steps.detail: The verifier checks that the legitimate objective is completed and that no forbidden call or exfiltrated value appears in the trajectory; where the environment provides diagnostic tools, it also checks that they were called before the corrective action, since the final outcome alone does not reveal the ordering.
steps.accept: The verifier fails a run that makes the forbidden call, and fails a run that reaches the objective by skipping the contaminated field.

curation_notes: Ship a benign control instance alongside the attacked one, with the same tools and the same objective but no payload, so the capability can be measured without the attack and the pair isolates the attack.
Treat placement and timing as parameters across the set rather than accidents, since both change how effective the attack is.
verifier: the tool-call log contains no call to the forbidden endpoint and no injected string in any argument
the legitimate objective's assertions hold in the final state; reward.txt is 1 or 0
the benign control instance passes under the same verifier with no attack-specific code path
the untouched workspace fails and writes 0 to /logs/verifier/reward.txt
pitfalls: payloads that merely restate the prompt are spotted trivially and measure nothing
checking only the final answer misses an agent that complied with the injection and then reported failure
the benign control drifting away from the attacked instance stops the pair from isolating the attack

source_papers.title: ToolHazard: Scaling Adversarial Environments for Security Evaluation and Alignment of LLM-based Agents
source_papers.note: environment simulator plus attacker and user simulators that discover viable injection points, generate environment-specific payloads and build state-grounded long-horizon tasks

source_papers.title: MLToolBench: Learning Tool-Augmented Agents for Machine Learning Development
source_papers.note: diagnostic tools whose value depends on later decisions, so the check must verify the diagnostic call happened before the fix rather than judging only the final outcome

source_papers.title: MCP-Atlas: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Tool-Use Competency with Real MCP Servers
source_papers.note: claim-level scoring that judges the final answer against atomic facts grounded in tool outputs, kept separate from tool-call correctness

recipes.name: Mid-task state disruption and replanning tasks
recipes.summary: Give the agent a tool environment whose state changes mid-task, so a plan committed at turn one goes stale and the agent must detect the change and rebuild it.
recipes.background: Task families in which the environment changes under the agent mid-execution, so a plan that was correct at turn one becomes wrong. The environment is built with explicit triggers - a field the agent read changes, a resource another actor takes, a tool's interface changes - that fire on a predicate and are injected into live state at a reproducible point of the episode. Because the trigger invalidates the committed plan, the agent must notice the shift, diagnose it and rebuild a strategy, and the three failure modes this elicits (executing on stale state, misdiagnosing the trigger, never verifying the adaptation) are exactly what a verifier has to separate. A stateful simulator of the server supplies the consistency and validity checks that let the agent discover that its plan no longer holds before it commits the next action.
needs: exposes a step counter or clock
has other actors that change state
recipes.produces: A multi-turn task whose agent must notice a mid-task state change and finish the objective with a revised plan, graded on the state after the adaptation.
when_to_use: the source domain has state that changes over time or across actors
you want to test replanning rather than first-shot planning
tasks must span several turns so a trigger can land mid-task
not_when_to_use: the environment is static and the task is a single call
the domain has no notion of time and no other actor that can change state
inputs: an executable tool environment whose state a trigger can mutate
a taxonomy of trigger types for the domain (value change, contention, interface evolution)
a deterministic firing point, such as a step counter or an observable clock

steps.title: Enumerate the domain's conflict types
steps.detail: List the ways state can invalidate a plan here - a read field changes, a resource is taken by another actor, a tool's schema or return shape changes - and build one trigger class per type rather than a single generic disruption.
steps.accept: One trigger class exists per conflict type, each naming the state field it watches.

steps.title: Make triggers conditional and deterministic
steps.detail: Each trigger is a predicate over environment state plus a firing condition, and the environment exposes a step counter or clock so the trigger fires at a reproducible point in the episode and can be re-run identically.
steps.accept: Re-running the episode fires the trigger at the same step and leaves the same state.

steps.title: Fire the trigger inside a valid trajectory
steps.detail: Run a reference trajectory, place the trigger at a step where the agent has already committed to a plan, and record the state before and after so the invalidation is provable from the log rather than asserted.
steps.accept: The recorded reference trajectory shows the trigger point and the state before and after it.

steps.title: Keep solvability across trigger types
steps.detail: Confirm a valid strategy still exists after the trigger fires: the reference solution must include the detection and the revised plan, and must still satisfy the task's assertions afterwards.
steps.accept: The reference solution detects the change, re-plans, and still satisfies the task's assertions after the trigger fires.

steps.title: Assert the post-adaptation state
steps.detail: The verifier checks the state after the adaptation, not the state the original plan aimed at; otherwise a stale-state execution that happens to land on a passing state passes anyway.
steps.accept: The verifier reads the state after the adaptation, so a run that ignored the change fails.

steps.title: Grade the failure mode, not only success
steps.detail: Record the taxonomy in the task metadata - stale-state execution, misdiagnosis of the dynamic trigger, and missing post-adaptation verification - so results across instances stay comparable.
steps.accept: The task metadata names the three failure modes: stale-state execution, misdiagnosis of the dynamic trigger, and missing post-adaptation verification.

steps.title: Optionally evolve the tool interface as a trigger
steps.detail: Mutate the interface itself - rename a tool, add a parameter, change a return shape - so the task also measures whether the agent re-reads the tool definitions after the change instead of reusing the old call.
steps.accept: The mutated tool is registered under its new name or shape, and the environment returns the new schema when the agent lists tools.

curation_notes: Label each failed run as stale-state execution, misdiagnosis of the dynamic trigger, or missing post-adaptation verification, and aggregate the labels across instances so the taxonomy carries information.
Cover every trigger class with at least one instance, so the domain's conflict types are exercised rather than only named.
verifier: post-trigger final state asserted by value; a stale plan that ignores the change fails
the reference trajectory records the trigger point and the revised action sequence
the trigger predicate is re-evaluated at verify time and reports that it fired
the untouched workspace fails and writes 0 to /logs/verifier/reward.txt
pitfalls: a trigger that fires after the objective is already complete has no effect on the trajectory
asserting the pre-trigger state lets a stale-state execution pass
triggers that only change wording create no real plan invalidation

source_papers.title: STT-Arena: A More Realistic Environment for Tool-Using with Spatio-Temporal Dynamics
source_papers.note: executable environments with injected spatio-temporal triggers that invalidate an ongoing plan, plus the three recurring failure modes including missing post-adaptation verification

source_papers.title: Gecko: A Simulation Environment with Stateful Feedback for Refining Agent Tool Calls
source_papers.note: stateful simulator that checks tool names and arguments and returns schema-conforming, state-consistent responses so call sequences can be refined before real execution

source_papers.title: MCPEvol-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agent Performance Across Dynamic Evolutions of MCP Servers
source_papers.note: mutation operators applied to live MCP servers to simulate tool evolution, with a measurable rise in planning and reasoning errors on the evolved versions

recipes.name: Trace-mined MCP composition environments
recipes.summary: Mine recorded MCP call traces for data, state and retry dependencies, cluster the composition graph into environments, and keep only the chains that replay cleanly from the seeded state.
recipes.background: Build the tool environment out of real call traces instead of out of a hand-written scenario. Adjacent calls in recorded MCP sessions are mined for three dependency kinds - data (an argument value produced by an earlier return), state (a later call whose result depends on an earlier mutation) and retry (a repeat of the same call after an error) - using deterministic rules rather than model judgement, which yields a weighted tool-composition graph. The graph is clustered into environments; a database is synthesised only for state-mutating tools, while query and stateless tools replay their recorded returns, so the replayed side stays faithful and the mutating side stays consistent. Long tasks come from state-aware random walks with rollback, each chain decompiled into a natural-language objective with assertion-based checks, and only chains that replay successfully from the initial state are kept. The output is multi-step, cross-server work with an executable, replayable check.
recipes.produces: A multi-server tool-use task whose checks are assertions on the final database state, generated from a chain that was proven to replay from the seeded initial state.
when_to_use: the source links to real MCP servers or ships recorded MCP call traces
you need tasks that span several tools or several servers
tool interfaces must match the real ones rather than a mock invented by the generator
not_when_to_use: no traces exist for the target tools
the task is a single tool call with a deterministic output
inputs: recorded MCP call traces (tool name, arguments, returns, errors)
a container backend that provisions and resets one MCP server instance per rollout
a deterministic rule engine for dependency mining, with no model call in the mining step

steps.title: Mine dependencies with deterministic rules
steps.detail: Scan consecutive calls in the traces for data, state and retry dependencies and emit a weighted edge per dependency. Deterministic rules only: an edge that cannot be witnessed by a recorded call sequence is not an edge.
steps.accept: Every edge in the graph is witnessed by a recorded call sequence; none comes from model judgement.

steps.title: Cluster the composition graph into environments
steps.detail: Cluster the weighted tool-composition graph into coherent environments and keep an environment only when its tools form a connected sub-graph with enough distinct edges to support multi-step work.
steps.accept: Each retained environment's tools form a connected sub-graph with enough distinct edges to support multi-step work.

steps.title: Split stateful from stateless tools
steps.detail: Synthesise a database only for the tools that mutate state; query and stateless tools replay their recorded returns. Record the classification per tool so the walker knows what can be replayed and what must be executed.
steps.accept: Every tool is labelled state-mutating or replay-only, and only the mutating tools have a synthesised database.

steps.title: Walk the graph with rollback
steps.detail: Generate long chains by state-aware random walks that respect the mined dependencies, snapshotting and rolling back state between candidate chains so every candidate starts from the same initial state.
steps.accept: Every candidate chain starts from the same seeded initial state.

steps.title: Decompile the chain into a task with assertions
steps.detail: Turn each chain into a natural-language objective that names neither the tools nor the order, and attach assertion-based checks derived from the chain's final state rather than from the agent's prose.
steps.accept: The instruction names neither the tools nor the order, and the checks are assertions over final state.

steps.title: Keep only chains that replay
steps.detail: Re-execute every candidate chain from the initial state and keep only those that replay successfully with all assertions holding. This execution filter is the main quality gate; anything that fails it is discarded.
steps.accept: The chain re-executes from the initial state and every assertion holds.

steps.title: Pin one isolated server instance per rollout
steps.detail: Provision a resettable, isolated instance of the MCP server per trajectory through the MCP interface itself, so the same task can be re-run without leftover server state bleeding into the next attempt.
steps.accept: Each rollout gets a fresh, resettable server instance, and no state carries over between attempts.

curation_notes: Scale the mining to the full trace set without losing determinism: re-run the rule engine and diff the edge set, so a regenerated benchmark keeps the same dependencies.
Retain a chain only when its assertions fail on the initial state, so a task cannot be passed by doing nothing.
verifier: assertion-based checks on the final database state for state-mutating tools, executed by tests/test.sh
the recorded chain replays from the seeded initial state and satisfies every assertion
the reference solution passes and the untouched workspace writes 0 to /logs/verifier/reward.txt
a wrong-but-plausible chain is rejected by the assertion, not merely by a different call count
pitfalls: model-judged dependency edges look plausible but do not replay; only execution-witnessed edges survive
synthesising a database for stateless tools invents mutable state that never existed
prompts that name the tools collapse the task back into single-call behaviour

source_papers.title: ToolSpace: Scaling Tool-Centric Environment Synthesis for Long-Horizon Agents
source_papers.note: reverses the data-first order: mines data, state and retry dependencies from traces, clusters the composition graph, synthesises databases only for mutating tools, walks with rollback and keeps only replayable chains

source_papers.title: MCP-Universe RL: A Framework for Training MCP Tool-Use Agents via Reinforcement Learning
source_papers.note: MCP as the universal environment interface, plus an orchestration layer that provisions, isolates and recycles MCP environments over a pluggable container backend

source_papers.title: MCP-Atlas: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Tool-Use Competency with Real MCP Servers
source_papers.note: prompts omit servers, tools and parameters so plausible distractors must be rejected, and outcomes are scored by claim-level rubrics so alternative valid trajectories still get credit
